newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica govt seen rejecting maize floor price call.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica govt seen rejecting maize floor price call.

text.p: Calls for South Africa to implement a floor price in the maize market next season were likely to be rejected by government, sources said on Tuesday.
They said Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom would oppose such a move as it would conflict with his twin ideals of moving to a free farming market and keeping staple food prices cheap.

"I cannot see him agreeing to a floor price due to the fact that he is very well known as a supporter of the free market," said Bertus van Heerden, a senior manager in Standard Bank's agricultural division.
Maize producers and co-operatives on Friday proposed at a meeting of industry representatives that a floor price of around 490 rand a tonne be fixed in the market from May next year.
But talks deadlocked when processors, traders and other maize buyers strongly opposed such an intervention and the agriculture minister was asked to make a ruling.
Hanekom's spokesman Helmut Schlenter told Reuters a decision was likely to be made by the end of the week.
Yellow maize for March 1997 delivery is currently trading around 610 rand a tonne on the South African Futures Exchange with white fetching 700 rand.

Hanekom has on numerous occasions backed a deregulated farming industry. In September he said: "Market forces should be the strongest determinant...The government will always play a role in marketing, for example, of exports but we will not have a single channel marketing system and fixed pricing."
Observers said Hanekom was also sensitive to consumers' needs, especially after this season's high prices.
"He will rather look to his voters' interests, especially as many households are poor," said an agricultural economist who asked not to be identified.

Others said a floor price would conflict with the spirit of agricultural marketing legislation passed last month which outlaws statutory market controls and accepts supply and demand as the best ways to ensure efficient resource allocation.
Although the new act does allow for market interventions, industry consensus is needed before any measure is adopted.

"I don't think Hanekom will go for a statutory floor price system or a floor price for the whole industry as the new act emphasises that things like that should have industry support," said Johan Willemse an independant agricultural economist.
Kit Le Clus, the producers' representative at Friday's meeting said a market safety net was necessary to protect producers against the risk of very low prices next season.
Prices are expected to fall sharply amid plentiful U.S. exports and an expected local bumper crop if good rains persist.
"If the crop is larger than eight million tonnes, prices could drop very rapidly to 400 rand or less a tonne," Le Clus told Reuters.

The effect of this would be "disastrous" as producers would steer away from planting maize, which if extreme, could mean South Africa would have to import maize at high prices. This would squeeze livestock producers, he said.
